q: What characterizes an overhanging beam?
o: It is fixed at both ends
It has only an internal support
Its ends extend beyond the supports
n: An overhanging beam extends beyond its supports at one or both ends.

s: Types of Beams According to Function
q: What is a grade beam?
o: The lowest spandrel of a building with no basement
A beam carrying a machine shaft between bearings
A roof beam spanning between two trusses
A beam over a door or window opening
ref: Types of Beams According to Function
n: A grade beam is the lowermost spandrel of a building without a basement.

q: What is one purpose of using strain?
o: To classify the type of support used
To measure water pressure in pipes
To predict deformation and check tolerances
To find the dead load of a floor
n: Strain helps predict allowable deformation and tolerances.

q: What is the deflection limit for roof or floor construction supporting non-structural elements likely to be damaged by large deflections?
n: Deflection limits: flat roofs L/180; floors L/360; roofs or floors supporting parts likely to be damaged L/480; not likely to be damaged L/240.

q: In terms of capacity, what makes a section over-reinforced?
o: Its steel could carry more tension than the concrete can resist in compression
Its concrete could carry more compression than the steel can take in tension
Its steel and concrete would fail at exactly the same load
It has steel near both the tension and the compression faces
n: With too much steel, the concrete crushes before the steel yields, so the failure comes without warning.

q: When is a storey considered stiffly irregular or a soft storey based on stiffness?
o: Below 70% of the storey above, or 80% of the three above
Drift at one end over 1.2 times the average
Strength below 80% of the storey above
Mass above 150% of an adjacent storey
n: The criterion is lateral stiffness below 70% of the storey above or below 80% of the average of the three storeys above.

q: A projection beyond a re-entrant corner is 4 m on a plan dimension of 24 m. Is this a re-entrant corner irregularity (limit 15%)?
n: The limit is exceeded when both projections are more than 15% of the plan dimension in that direction.

q: What does strain represent?
n: Strain is the ratio of change in length to original length, written ΔL/L.

q: What long-to-short side ratio identifies a two-way slab?
n: A two-way slab is identified when the long-to-short side ratio is less than 2.

q: How is an axial load applied relative to a member?
o: Only through its center of gravity
n: An axial load acts parallel to the member's length.

q: A storey has 68% of the lateral stiffness of the storey above. Which irregularity is this?
n: A soft storey is less than 70% as stiff as the storey above, or less than 80% of the average of the three above.

q: A material has a stress of 200 MPa at a strain of 0.001. What is its modulus of elasticity?
n: E is stress divided by strain; 200,000 MPa (200 GPa) is the value for steel.

q: How is the modulus of elasticity expressed?
n: The modulus of elasticity is expressed as stress over strain, σ/ε.

q: Which structural system has no vertical load-carrying space frame and therefore has no beams or columns?
n: The bearing wall system is described as lacking a vertical load-carrying space frame, with no beams or columns.

q: Which forces does a surface-active structure, such as a shell, mainly resist?
n: Shells and folded plates carry load as in-plane (membrane) forces spread over their surface.

q: What behavior is associated with a long column?
n: Long columns carry compression and bending and are primarily associated with buckling.

q: Which set lists only truss types?
n: Barrels, ribs, domes, shells and buttresses are other structural forms, not trusses.

q: At what point does plastic deformation begin?
n: The yield point marks the beginning of plastic deformation.

q: Why might an architect use doubly reinforced concrete when member dimensions are limited?
o: To avoid using steel in the tension zone
To carry more moment in a small section
To remove the need for any stirrups
To allow a lower concrete strength
n: Doubly reinforced members are useful when the architect limits the sectional dimensions and additional capacity is needed.

q: What distinguishes the structural action considered in a two-way slab?
o: Moment is considered in both directions
Moment is considered only along the short side
n: Two-way slab design considers moment in both directions.

q: The maximum storey drift at one end is 18 mm and the average storey drift is 14 mm. Is this a torsional irregularity (limit 1.2 times the average)?
o: No; the drifts must be equal
n: Torsional irregularity exists when the drift at one end exceeds 1.2 times the average of the drifts at the two ends.

q: Which load is distributed at a constant intensity?
n: A uniformly distributed load has a constant load intensity over its loaded length or area.

q: When does torsional irregularity occur?
o: When the drift at one end exceeds 2.0 times the average drift
When the drift at one end is below 0.8 times the average
When the drift at one end exceeds 1.2 times the average drift
When the drift at both ends is equal
n: Uneven drift means the building twists about a vertical axis.

q: What is the fracture point?
o: The point where stress becomes proportional to strain
The stress at which fracture failure occurs
n: The fracture point is the stress level at which the material fails by fracture.

s: Types of Beams According to Function
q: Which beam is a large member that carries floor beams?
ref: Types of Beams According to Function
n: A girder is a large beam that carries floor beams.

q: When are tendons tensioned in pre-tensioned concrete?
n: In pre-tensioned concrete, the tendons are stressed before the concrete is cast.

q: How does an over-reinforced section fail?
n: Over-reinforced sections fail by crushing in the compression zone, and the failure is described as instantaneous.

q: What capacity relationship defines an under-reinforced section?
o: Tension capacity is greater than compression capacity
Tension capacity is smaller than compression capacity
n: An under-reinforced section has lower tension capacity than compression capacity.

q: Which is an example of a form-active structure?
n: Tensile fabric and arches are the examples given for form-active structures.

q: A load applied at one location is classified by distribution as what?
n: A concentrated or point load acts at a specific location rather than being spread continuously.

q: A rectangular slab measures 8 m by 3 m. How is it classified?
n: A long-to-short ratio above 2 makes a one-way slab; 2 or less, two-way.
steps: 2.67 > 2, so it bends mainly one way

q: Which symbol usually stands for shear force in beam diagrams?
n: V is shear, M is moment, E is modulus of elasticity.

q: Where are the supports of a simple span beam located?
o: At the ends of the span
n: A simple span beam has supports located at the ends of its span.

q: Which design method uses the elastic limit of materials?
n: Working Stress Design is based on the elastic limit of the materials and is identified as no longer used.

q: What is another name for ultimate strength in tension?
n: It is also called ultimate strength the ultimate tensile strength.

q: What characterizes doubly reinforced concrete?
o: Reinforcement is provided near both tensile and compressive faces
Reinforcement is provided only near the tensile face
Reinforcement is placed only in the middle
n: Doubly reinforced concrete adds reinforcement near the compressive face in addition to the tensile reinforcement.

q: What condition defines translational equilibrium?
o: The sum of forces is zero
The sum of moments is zero
n: Translational equilibrium requires the vector sum of the external forces to equal zero.

q: What is the deflection limit for floors not supporting elements likely to be damaged by large deflections?
n: Deflection limits: flat roofs L/180; floors L/360; roofs or floors supporting parts likely to be damaged L/480; not likely to be damaged L/240.

q: Which force does a vector-active structure, such as a truss, mainly resist in its members?
n: Truss members are pin-jointed, so each carries only tension or compression.

q: A force acts perpendicular to the length of a beam. What is it, and what can it cause?
o: An axial load; compression or tension
A point load; axial force only
A dead load; no internal forces
A transverse (lateral) load; shear, bending or torsion
n: A load across a member bends it and shears it; if it is off-center, it also twists it.

q: A floor member supporting partitions likely to crack spans 7,200 mm. With the L/480 limit, what is its allowable deflection?
n: Deflection limits: flat roofs L/180; floors L/360; roofs or floors supporting parts likely to be damaged L/480; not likely to be damaged L/240.

q: Which stress governs an under-reinforced section?
o: Ultimate stress of the concrete only
n: The yield stress of the reinforcement governs the under-reinforced condition.

q: A structure made of rigid surfaces that redirect loads through its shape is classified as what?
n: Surface-active systems use rigid surfaces whose shape redirects applied loads.

q: A 2,000 mm long member elongates by 2 mm. What is its strain?
n: Strain is change in length over original length; it has no units.

q: What condition defines rotational equilibrium?
o: Vector sum of forces equals zero
Total torque or moment equals zero
n: Rotational equilibrium requires the total torque or moment acting on the object to equal zero.

q: A storey has an effective mass of 480 tonnes and an adjacent storey 300 tonnes. Is this a mass irregularity (limit 150%)?
n: Mass irregularity exists when a storey's mass exceeds 150% of an adjacent storey's.
steps: 160% > 150%, so it is a mass irregularity

q: Which force does a form-active structure, such as a cable or arch, mainly carry?
n: The shape follows the load path, so a cable is in pure tension and an ideal arch in pure compression.

q: Which behavior is associated with a ductile material such as steel before failure?
n: Ductile materials such as steel experience necking before failure.

q: A storey has 75% of the stiffness of the storey above and 82% of the average of the three above. Is it a soft storey?
o: No; it passes both limits (70% and 80%)
Yes; any drop in stiffness counts
n: It would be soft only below 70% of the storey above or below 80% of the three-storey average.

q: What two internal force effects are highlighted for beams?
n: The beam section notes simultaneous compression and tension, along with vertical force and bending moment.

q: Which support restrains horizontal and vertical movement but allows rotation?
ref: Types of Supports for Coplanar Systems
n: A pin support restrains horizontal and vertical translation while permitting rotation.

q: Which combinations are possible within the force-system classifications?
n: Both coplanar and spatial systems may contain concurrent, parallel, non-concurrent, or non-parallel forces.

q: What cover range is specified for slabs, walls, and joists not exposed to weather?
n: Slabs, walls, and joists not exposed to weather are assigned 20–40 mm of cover.

q: What distinguishes a 2D or coplanar force system?
n: A 2D or coplanar system contains forces acting on two axes and may be concurrent, parallel, non-concurrent, or non-parallel.

q: Besides the Warren and K-truss, which two are common truss types?
n: Scissor trusses have sloping bottom chords; bowstring trusses have a curved top chord.

q: What is strength in the context of materials?
o: The ability to remain intact under forces
The ability to change color under heat
n: Strength is the ability of a material to hold itself together while subjected to forces.

q: What is one purpose of using stress?
o: To predict when a material may break
n: Stress is used to evaluate material response and help predict when a material will break.

q: What defines weight or mass irregularity?
o: Effective mass of a storey is more than 150% of an adjacent storey
Effective mass is below 70% of the storey above
n: Weight or mass irregularity occurs when a storey's effective mass exceeds 150% of an adjacent storey.

q: When are tendons tensioned in post-tensioned concrete?
n: Post-tensioned tendons are stressed after the concrete has been cast.

q: What characterizes an in-plane discontinuity?
o: A sideways offset of lateral-resisting elements
A storey mass above 150% of the next
A sudden change in roof height
A drift above 1.2 times the average
n: An in-plane discontinuity is an offset in the plane of lateral-resisting structural elements.

q: What does statics study?
o: Bodies at rest under balanced forces
n: Statics deals with objects subjected to forces while remaining in static equilibrium.

q: What distinguishes a 3D or spatial force system?
o: Forces occur only at right angles
n: A spatial system contains forces acting on three axes and may have different concurrency and direction relationships.

q: What is the effective length factor K of a column fixed at the base and free at the top?
n: Fixed-fixed 0.5, fixed-pinned 0.7, pinned-pinned 1.0, fixed-free (flagpole) 2.0.

s: Types of Beams According to Function
q: Which member transmits power to machinery and also carries torsion, shear, and flexure?
ref: Types of Beams According to Function
n: The shaft is a circular beam that transmits power and carries torsion in addition to shear and flexure.

q: When do re-entrant corners make a plan irregular?
o: When projections beyond the corner exceed 15% of the plan dimension
When projections exceed 5% of the plan dimension
When projections exceed 50% of the plan dimension
Whenever the building has any corner
n: L-, T- and U-shaped plans concentrate stress at the inside corner.

q: What stress and failure are associated with a short column?
n: A short column is described as carrying compression and failing by crushing.

s: Types of Beams According to Function
q: Which beam carries masonry over door and window openings?
ref: Types of Beams According to Function
n: A lintel supports masonry across openings such as doors and windows.

q: What movement is permitted between idealized truss members at a pin joint?
o: Members may rotate relative to one another
n: Pin connections allow the connected truss members to rotate relative to one another.

q: What does stress represent in the simplified definition?
o: Change in length divided by length
n: Stress is given by force over area, F/A.

q: A beam end resting on a wall, free to rotate and slide, is modeled as which support?
n: A simple (roller-type) support gives only a vertical reaction.

q: What is the main subject of strength of materials?
o: External loads on a building only
n: Strength of materials examines how external forces create internal effects within materials and structural members.

q: Which system combines moment-resisting frames with shear walls or braced frames?
n: The dual system combines moment-resisting frames with shear walls or braced frames.

q: Which system uses a complete space frame for gravity loads while shear walls and braced frames resist lateral loads?
n: In the building frame system, the space frame carries gravity loads while shear walls and brace frames resist lateral loads.

q: In a Pratt truss, how are the diagonals and verticals oriented in terms of force?
o: Diagonals in tension; verticals in compression
Diagonals in compression; verticals in tension
n: A Pratt truss reverses the force pattern: the diagonals are in tension and the verticals in compression.

q: A member carries an axial force of 24 kN on a cross-section of 1,200 mm². What is the stress?
n: 1 N/mm² = 1 MPa.

q: Why is a balanced design described as risky?
o: It always fails in tension first
It has no reinforcement at all
It cannot carry any dead load
It can fail by crushing without warning
n: Balanced behavior is considered risky because, like an over-reinforced section, failure is sudden and gives little early warning.

q: What happens up to the proportionality limit?
n: Up to the proportionality limit, stress and strain remain proportional in accordance with Hooke's Law.

q: A member supporting elements not likely to be damaged by large deflection spans 6,000 mm. With the L/240 limit, what is its allowable deflection?
n: Deflection limits: flat roofs L/180; floors L/360; roofs or floors supporting parts likely to be damaged L/480; not likely to be damaged L/240.

q: In a one-way slab, where is moment-resisting reinforcement placed?
n: The definition states that moment-resisting reinforcement in a one-way slab runs along the short side.

q: Which classification is based on how a load is spread over a member?
n: The load categories concentrated, uniformly distributed, and uniformly varying are grouped by distribution.

q: What is the effective length factor K of a column fixed at both ends?
n: Fixing both ends halves the buckling length.

q: A building's own weight is classified under which load category?
n: The weight of the structure itself is identified as a dead or static load.

q: A flat roof member spans 5,400 mm. With the L/180 limit, what is its allowable deflection?
n: Deflection limits: flat roofs L/180; floors L/360; roofs or floors supporting parts likely to be damaged L/480; not likely to be damaged L/240.

q: What is a basic strength characteristic of concrete?
o: Low compressive strength and high tensile strength
High compressive strength and low tensile strength
n: Concrete is characterized by high compressive strength but relatively low tensile strength.

q: What is ultimate strength?
n: Ultimate strength is the maximum stress a material reaches while being stretched before breaking.

q: Where should the building configuration ideally keep its mass in relation to the center of gravity?
o: Far from the center of gravity
n: The preferred configuration keeps the structure near its center of gravity.

q: Which pair is used to describe force intensity and deformation behavior?
n: Stress describes force intensity over area, while strain describes deformation relative to original length.

q: Which system uses flexural action members to resist lateral loads?
n: Moment-resisting frames use flexural action in their members to resist lateral loads.

q: How are truss members ideally connected at the joints?
n: The idealized truss uses frictionless pins at the joints.

q: Why is steel reinforcement commonly used in concrete?
o: It adds the tensile strength concrete lacks
It removes all compression from the concrete
It eliminates the dead load of the member
It prevents every kind of cracking
n: Steel reinforcement supplements the tensile capacity that concrete lacks.

q: A simply supported beam carries a single 12 kN load at midspan. What is each support reaction?
n: A symmetric load splits equally.

s: Types of Beams According to Function
q: Which member is usually sloped and carries loads from purlins?
ref: Types of Beams According to Function
n: A rafter is usually sloping and carries the load from purlins.

q: A structure whose material naturally deflects and stabilizes under loading is what type?
n: Form-active systems rely on the natural deflected shape of the material to achieve stability.

q: How does fracture strength compare with ultimate strength in a ductile material such as steel?
n: For ductile materials, fracture strength is lower than ultimate strength because necking occurs before failure.

q: Which truss type is specifically identified with vertical members in its name?
n: The named type is Warren truss (with vertical).

q: Which symbol is used for bending moment?
n: Bending moment is denoted by M.

q: What governs the strength of an over-reinforced section?
o: The compressive strength of the concrete
The yield strength of the steel
The tensile strength of the concrete
The shear strength of the stirrups
n: The concrete crushes (at a strain of about 0.003) before the steel reaches yield.

q: People, furniture, and wind are examples of what type of load?
n: People, furniture, and wind are transient or moving actions categorized as live or dynamic loads.

q: Which branch of mechanics deals with fluids?
n: Fluid mechanics focuses on bodies or systems in which the material behaves as a fluid.

q: Which support allows movement horizontally while resisting vertical movement?
ref: Types of Supports for Coplanar Systems
n: The roller support permits horizontal movement and resists vertical movement.

q: A storey has 85% of the stiffness of the storey above but 76% of the average of the three above. Is it a soft storey?
o: Yes; 76% is below the 80% average limit
n: Failing either test (below 70% of the storey above, or below 80% of the three-storey average) makes it soft.

q: In a Howe truss, how are the diagonals and verticals oriented in terms of force?
o: Diagonals in tension; verticals in compression
Diagonals in compression; verticals in tension
n: A Howe truss has diagonals in compression and vertical members in tension.

q: Which configuration feature is preferred because it keeps the structure's geometry more regular?
n: The preferred configuration uses fewer reentrant angles to maintain a more regular structural form.

q: Which structural category transfers loads through interlinked components whose geometry and orientation matter?
n: Vector-active structures transfer loads through linked components and depend on their geometry and orientation.

q: What cover do cast-in-place members exposed to weather need for bars 16 mm and smaller?
n: Exposed to weather or earth: 40 mm for bars up to 16 mm, 50 mm for 20 mm bars and larger.

q: Which pair consists of vector-active examples?
n: Geodesic domes and trusses are examples of vector-active systems.

q: Which deflection limit is the strictest?
o: L/240, for elements not likely to be damaged
L/480, for construction supporting easily damaged elements
n: Deflection limits: flat roofs L/180; floors L/360; roofs or floors supporting parts likely to be damaged L/480; not likely to be damaged L/240.

s: Types of Beams According to Function
q: Which beam consists of closely spaced members supporting a floor or ceiling?
ref: Types of Beams According to Function
n: Joists are closely spaced beams that support floors or ceilings.

q: Which forces does a section-active structure, such as a frame, resist?
n: Beams and columns carry load through the strength of their cross-sections, so they take every kind of internal force.

q: What concrete cover is given for reinforcement exposed directly to earth, such as footings?
n: The specified concrete cover for reinforcement exposed to earth, such as footings, is 75 mm.

q: What behavior is associated with an intermediate column?
o: Compression only; yielding of the concrete
Shear and torsion; twisting of the section
Tension only; fracture of the bars
Compression and bending; crushing or buckling
n: Intermediate columns experience compression and bending and may fail by crushing or buckling.

q: Which actions are idealized as not being resisted directly by a truss?
n: The idealized truss is described as incapable of resisting bending, moment, and shear.

q: A footing bar will be cast against earth. What concrete cover is needed?
n: Concrete cast against and permanently exposed to earth needs 75 mm.

q: What cover is specified for beams and columns not exposed to weather?
n: The specified cover for beams and columns not exposed to weather is 40 mm.

q: How does fracture strength compare with ultimate strength in a brittle material such as concrete?
n: For brittle materials such as concrete, the fracture strength is identified as equivalent to ultimate strength.

q: Which branch treats an object as a rigid body when analyzing its motion or equilibrium?
n: Rigid body mechanics idealizes the object as not undergoing significant deformation during the analysis.

q: A storey has a lateral strength of 720 kN; the storey above has 1,000 kN. Which irregularity applies?
n: A weak storey has less than 80% of the strength of the storey above.
steps: 72% < 80%, so it is a weak storey

s: Types of Beams According to Function
q: Which beam carries roof loads between trusses or rafters?
ref: Types of Beams According to Function
n: A purlin carries roof load between trusses or rafters.

q: A 10 kN load acts 2 m from the left support of a 6 m simply supported beam. What is the right support reaction?
n: Take moments about the left support.

q: Which load changes in intensity across its loaded length?
n: A uniformly varying load changes continuously in intensity across the loaded region.

q: Which branch studies bodies that change shape under loading?
n: Deformed body mechanics considers bodies whose shape changes under applied forces.

q: Which support provides resistance against horizontal movement, vertical movement, and rotation?
n: A fixed support restrains horizontal translation, vertical translation, and rotation.

q: What is the deflection limit for construction supporting elements not likely to be damaged by large deflections?
n: Deflection limits: flat roofs L/180; floors L/360; roofs or floors supporting parts likely to be damaged L/480; not likely to be damaged L/240.

q: How does an under-reinforced section fail?
o: The concrete crushes instantly without warning
The section fails only in shear
The reinforcement yields in a ductile manner
n: An under-reinforced section yields in a ductile manner, producing large visible deformation before failure.

q: What concrete cover range is given for reinforcement exposed to weather?
n: Reinforcement exposed to weather is assigned a cover of 40–50 mm.

q: Which combination of effects may result from a lateral load?
n: The definition states that lateral loading can induce shear, bending, and/or torsion.

q: What condition causes a building to fail in the sense of statics?
o: It has a low center of gravity
It is not in static equilibrium
n: A structure must satisfy ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0; if it cannot, it moves, overturns or collapses.

q: What are the two main divisions of mechanics?
n: Statics studies bodies at rest; dynamics studies bodies in motion.

q: Which system relies on cantilevered column elements to resist lateral loads?
n: The cantilevered column building system relies on cantilevered columns to resist lateral loads.

q: What characterizes a cantilever beam?
o: It is curved along its whole length
It is supported at both of its ends
It is fixed at one end and free at the other
It rests on three or more supports
n: A cantilever is supported at only one end through a rigid connection.

q: Which support restrains horizontal movement, vertical movement, and rotation?
ref: Types of Supports for Coplanar Systems
n: A fixed support resists all three specified motions: horizontal, vertical, and rotational.

q: What long-to-short side ratio identifies a one-way slab?
n: A one-way slab is identified when the long-to-short side ratio is greater than 2.

q: Which example is identified as surface active?
n: Concrete shells are given as the representative surface-active example.

q: Which building configuration is considered structurally preferable?
o: Maximum distance from the center of gravity
Structurally symmetrical with fewer reentrant angles
n: The preferred configuration is structurally symmetrical, has fewer reentrant angles, and keeps the mass close to the center of gravity.

q: What defines diaphragm discontinuity?
o: A diaphragm has abrupt variations in stiffness
The roof has a constant slope
n: Diaphragm discontinuity refers to abrupt variations in diaphragm stiffness.

q: What is the significance of the elastic limit?
o: It is where stiffness becomes infinite
n: Passing the elastic limit means the material will no longer return fully to its original shape.

q: Which set contains the main considerations in strength of materials?
o: Cost, labor supply and construction schedule
Heat, light and sound in the building
Color, texture and finish of members
Material and section properties, and connections
n: The main considerations are material properties, sectional properties, and proper connectors.

q: What is an out-of-plane offset?
o: A discontinuity in the lateral-force path
n: An out-of-plane offset is described as a discontinuity in the lateral force path.

q: What does the modulus of elasticity describe?
n: The modulus of elasticity, E, describes a material's stiffness.

q: Which design method uses the ultimate strength of materials?
n: Ultimate Stress Design uses the ultimate strength or failure condition and better reflects actual material behavior.

q: What does mechanics examine?
n: Mechanics examines objects at rest or in motion when forces act on them.

q: What characterizes a continuous beam?
o: It has no support at the ends
It is supported at more than two points
It is supported only at one end
n: A continuous beam is supported at more than two points along its span.

q: What is the deflection limit for flat roofs not supporting elements likely to be damaged?
n: Deflection limits: flat roofs L/180; floors L/360; roofs or floors supporting parts likely to be damaged L/480; not likely to be damaged L/240.

q: What defines a discontinuity in capacity or weak storey?
o: Storey mass is more than 150% of an adjacent storey
Storey strength is less than 80% of the storey above
n: A weak storey is identified when its strength is below 80% of the storey above.

q: What characterizes singly reinforced concrete?
o: Reinforcement is placed only near the compressive face
Reinforcement is placed only near the tensile face
Equal reinforcement is placed on all faces
n: Singly reinforced concrete is reinforced near the tensile face only.

q: A structure dependent on the sectional properties of rigid components is classified as what?
n: Section-active systems depend on the sectional properties of rigid components.

q: Why must a beam develop internal resisting forces?
o: To avoid the need for any supports
To balance the effects of external loads
To increase the dead load it carries
To remove every bit of deformation
n: Internal resisting forces balance the internally developed forces resulting from externally applied forces.

q: A floor beam spans 7,200 mm. With the L/360 limit, what is its allowable deflection?
n: Deflection limits: flat roofs L/180; floors L/360; roofs or floors supporting parts likely to be damaged L/480; not likely to be damaged L/240.

q: What kind of load is a beam mainly designed to carry?
n: Beams carry transverse loads by bending and shear.

s: Types of Beams According to Function
q: Which member carries the flooring of a bridge, such as at stairs?
ref: Types of Beams According to Function
n: A stringer carries the flooring of a bridge and is used in applications such as stairs.

q: What actions can an axial load induce?
n: Axial loading produces compression or tension along the member.

q: What defines a non-parallel system?
o: Lateral-resisting elements not parallel to the main axes
All elements parallel to one main axis
Only columns offset from floor to floor
A structure with a circular plan
n: A non-parallel system has vertical lateral-load-resisting elements that are not parallel or symmetric about the major orthogonal axes.

q: Which system combines shear walls and frames so lateral forces are shared in proportion to their relative rigidities?
n: The interactive system combines shear walls and frames, distributing lateral forces in proportion to their relative rigidities.

q: What defines a balanced design?
o: Tension capacity is twice compression capacity
Tensile and compressive zones fail at the same load
n: Balanced design is defined as the tensile and compressive zones reaching failure at the same load.

q: Which example represents a section-active structure?
n: Steel and column frames are given as examples of section-active structures.

q: How is a lateral load applied?
n: A lateral load acts perpendicular or transverse to the member's length.

s: Types of Beams According to Function
q: Which beam spans between columns and supports floors and curtain walls?
ref: Types of Beams According to Function
n: A spandrel spans between columns and supports floors and curtain walls.

q: Why is the circle favored as a basic structural geometry?
o: It needs no connectors between parts
It uses the least material of any shape
It eliminates bending in every case
Every point is equally far from its center
n: The circle keeps every point at the same distance from the center of gravity.

q: What geometric form is identified as the best basic geometry for structural stability?
n: A circle is identified as the best geometry because every point is equidistant from the center of gravity.
